passage: Ammi held out the spoon. "Bhindi, Zeenat?" Zeenat, two, clamped her lips and turned her face into the chair. "No." Across the mat, her cousin Dilnaz, four, crunched a piece loudly. "Mmm! Crispy!" Zeenat stared. Dilnaz took another and grinned, green bits on her chin. "More, Khala, please." Zeenat pointed at Dilnaz's plate. "That." "The same bhindi?" Ammi asked, smiling. Zeenat opened her mouth, chewed slowly, then held out her hand for more.

qa.q: What vegetable did Ammi offer Zeenat?
qa.a: Bhindi.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's long stare at Dilnaz suggest?
qa.a: Zeenat seems curious and less wary; watching Dilnaz enjoy the bhindi made the strange food look safe to try.

qa.q: What changed Zeenat's mind, and how could Ammi use that at the next meal?
qa.a: Seeing Dilnaz eat happily was the turning point, so Ammi could seat Zeenat beside a child enjoying a new food instead of pushing the spoon. 🙂

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel about being watched and copied?
qa.a: Dilnaz is simply enjoying the snack, but being copied may feel nice, like being the big cousin who shows the way.

grounding: A toddler refuses a food until an older cousin eats it happily, then tries it.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. At snack time Ojas (2) pushed away the steamed carrot sticks again: "No, no." I didn't press. Trisha sat beside him, dipped a stick in curd and crunched it, swinging her legs. "Yum!" Ojas watched her for a long moment, then licked one stick and bit the end. He ate three more, glancing at Trisha after each bite. Plan: seat Ojas next to Trisha when new foods come out this week, and tell his parents what helped. — Ms Lobo

qa.q: What food did Ojas push away at snack time?
qa.a: The steamed carrot sticks.

qa.q: What might Ojas's glance at Trisha after each bite suggest?
qa.a: Ojas seems to be checking that it is still okay; Trisha's happy crunching is reassuring about this new food.

qa.q: What choice did Ms Lobo make when Ojas refused, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ms Lobo didn't press, which left room for Ojas to watch Trisha and try the carrots without a fight.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha had pulled a face at the carrots?
qa.a: Ojas would probably have kept refusing, because Trisha's enjoyment was the cue Ojas was reading.

grounding: A daycare note records a toddler trying carrots only after watching another child eat them happily.

passage: Under the neem tree in Nani's courtyard sat a basket of jamun. Payal, almost three, poked one and pulled her finger back. Too dark, too squishy. Nani held one out; Payal hid behind the charpai. Then Vandana from next door skipped in, popped two into her mouth and stuck out a bright purple tongue. "Sweet!" Payal giggled. She crept out, took the smallest jamun, and bit it with her eyes squeezed shut. Then she stuck out her own purple tongue at Vandana.

qa.q: Where was the basket of jamun?
qa.a: Under the neem tree in Nani's courtyard.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling as she bit the jamun with her eyes squeezed shut?
qa.a: Payal was still a little nervous, but brave enough to try now that Vandana had enjoyed the fruit.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Payal, and what could Nani try with other new fruits?
qa.a: The turning point was Vandana eating happily and showing a purple tongue; Nani could invite Vandana over when offering Payal something new.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Payal's purple tongue at the end?
qa.a: To Vandana it probably feels like a shared joke and the start of a game, since Payal copied the tongue trick back.

grounding: A toddler in a village tries jamun only after a neighbour child eats it with delight.

passage: Saturday playgroup, a park in Porto. Paulo, two, pressed his lips shut when his dad held out a slice of kiwi. Green, fuzzy, strange. He pushed the hand away. On the blanket beside him, Soo-ah, three, bit into her own slice, juice dripping down her wrist. "Mmm!" she hummed, and grabbed another. Paulo watched her chew. He shuffled closer and watched again. Then he took the kiwi from his dad's palm, licked it, and bit. He held out his hand for more.

qa.q: What fruit did Paulo's dad offer him?
qa.a: His dad held out a slice of kiwi.

qa.q: What does Paulo shuffling closer and watching Soo-ah again suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He was curious but still unsure; seeing Soo-ah enjoy the kiwi seemed to tell him it was safe to try.

qa.q: What could Paulo's dad try the next time Paulo refuses a new fruit?
qa.a: He could sit Paulo near a child who is happily eating it and let him watch, without pushing the food at him.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel if she noticed Paulo copying her and asking for more?
qa.a: She might feel proud and grown-up, like she had shown a younger child something good.

grounding: It shows a toddler trying a new food only after watching another child eat it happily.

passage: I'm Sudha. I was holding my little brother Tanvir on the sea wall when Papa bought roasted corn from the cart. Tanvir is two. He shoved the cob away and hid his face in my kurta. Then a small girl beside us started gnawing hers, grinning, butter on her cheeks. Tanvir peeked. He stared at her for ages. Then he grabbed the cob and bit once, eyes still on her. I can't say what changed his mind, but he finished half.

qa.q: Where was Sudha holding Tanvir when Papa bought the corn?
qa.a: Sudha was holding Tanvir on the sea wall.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have kept his eyes on the girl while he took his first bite?
qa.a: He seemed to be checking her face for reassurance, because her happy chewing made the strange cob look safe to him.

qa.q: How could Sudha or Papa use what they saw the next time Tanvir refuses a food?
qa.a: They could let him sit with other children eating it happily instead of pushing it at him.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he sees Tanvir finish half the corn after refusing it?
qa.a: Papa might be surprised and relieved, and a little amused that a stranger's grin worked where his offer didn't.

grounding: An older sister observes a toddler eat a new food only after seeing another child enjoy it.

passage:
Monday. Mumma put mashed pumpkin on Kishore's plate. He pushed it away and shook his head.
Wednesday. At daycare, Kishore sat next to Avni. Avni scooped pumpkin with both hands, smacked her lips and laughed. Kishore watched her. He poked his pumpkin with one finger.
Friday. Avni ate her pumpkin again. Kishore looked at her, then picked up his spoon and took a bite. Then another. He held the spoon up to show Avni.

qa.q: What did Kishore do with the pumpkin on Monday?
qa.a: He pushed it away and shook his head.

qa.q: Why did Kishore finally take a bite on Friday?
qa.a: He felt safe and curious after watching Avni happily eat pumpkin again and again, so it seemed worth trying.

qa.q: How could grown-ups use this to help Kishore try new foods?
qa.a: They could seat him near children who enjoy the food and let him watch, without pushing him to eat.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when Kishore holds up his spoon?
qa.a: Avni might feel happy and proud, as if they are eating together.

grounding: A toddler tries pumpkin only after watching another child eat it happily over several days.

passage:
It was Lohri evening, and the Delhi society lawn was full of families round the fire. Gurleen sat on Mummy's lap, holding a piece of gajak. She turned it over and didn't bite.
Her cousin Chetan, a bit bigger, crunched his gajak loudly and grinned, sugar on his chin. Gurleen watched his mouth. She watched him take another bite.
Then she lifted hers and nibbled a corner. Her eyes went wide. She took a big bite and held out her hand to Mummy for more.

qa.q: What was Chetan eating?
qa.a: Chetan was eating gajak.

qa.q: What made Gurleen decide to nibble the gajak?
qa.a: She felt curious and reassured watching Chetan crunch it happily, which told her it was safe and good.

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time Gurleen is unsure of a food?
qa.a: Mummy could let her sit near a child who is enjoying the food and give her time to watch.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel with Gurleen watching him eat?
qa.a: Chetan might feel pleased and a little important, grinning as his younger cousin copies him.

grounding: A toddler tries gajak at a Lohri gathering only after watching her cousin eat it happily.

passage:
"Kashish, try the idli," said Amma at the Onam lunch. Kashish pressed her lips shut.
"Look, Naveen is eating," said Amma.
Naveen, across the banana leaf, stuffed a whole idli in his mouth. "Mmm!"
Kashish stared at him.
"Mmm!" said Naveen again, and took another.
Kashish picked up a small piece. She put it in her mouth. "Mmm," she said.
Amma laughed. "More?"
Kashish nodded and pointed at Naveen's leaf.

qa.q: What did Naveen stuff in his mouth?
qa.a: Naveen stuffed a whole idli in his mouth.

qa.q: Why did Kashish open her mouth for the idli after watching Naveen?
qa.a: She felt curious and safe, because seeing Naveen enjoy it showed her the idli was good.

qa.q: What worked better than Amma's first request?
qa.a: Letting Kashish watch Naveen eat happily worked better than just asking her to try.

qa.q: How might Amma feel when Kashish says "Mmm"?
qa.a: Amma probably feels delighted and relieved that Kashish finally tried the idli.

grounding: A toddler tries idli at an Onam lunch only after watching another child eat it happily.

passage:
Creche note, winter week. Manjula, caregiver.
Today we served carrot halwa for the first time. Mohit pushed his bowl away and shook his head. Then he watched the little girl beside him scoop it up, smile and hold out her bowl for more. Mohit leaned over, looked at her bowl, then at his own. He took one tiny spoonful. Then another. By the end his bowl was empty and his chin was orange.
Tomorrow I'll seat him beside her again when we try beetroot.

qa.q: What food was served for the first time?
qa.a: Carrot halwa.

qa.q: Why did Mohit try the halwa after pushing it away?
qa.a: Watching the girl beside him eat it happily made it seem safe, so his wariness turned into curiosity.

qa.q: How does Manjula plan to use what happened?
qa.a: Manjula plans to seat Mohit beside the same girl when they try beetroot.

qa.q: How might the little girl feel when Mohit copies her?
qa.a: She may feel pleased, or not notice at all, simply enjoying her halwa.

grounding: A caregiver's winter note shows a toddler trying a new food only after seeing another child eat it happily.

passage:
At Makar Sankranti, the village courtyard smelled of sesame and jaggery. Kashish's Nani held out a til laddoo. Kashish turned his face into her shoulder.
Across the mat, his cousin Irawati bit into one, crunched loudly and laughed with sticky fingers. Kashish peeked. He watched her take a second bite. Slowly he reached out, touched the laddoo and licked his finger. Then he held out his hand for more.

qa.a: A til laddoo.

qa.q: What made Kashish reach for the laddoo?
qa.a: Seeing Irawati crunch happily made it seem safe and fun, so his shyness turned into interest.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Kashish holds out his hand for more?
qa.a: She likely feels amused and pleased that he tried it.

grounding: Shows a toddler at a festival refusing a new sweet until he sees his cousin enjoy it, then trying it himself.

passage:
At the summer festival in the Kyoto park, the air was hot and full of drums. Aiko's father offered her a spoonful of green shaved ice. Aiko pressed her lips shut.
On the bench, a little girl called Nour was eating the same ice, giggling at the cold and kicking her legs. Aiko stared. Nour's mother gave her another spoonful, and Nour squealed happily.
Aiko opened her mouth for her father's spoon. Her eyes went wide at the cold. Then she reached for more.

qa.q: What colour was the shaved ice?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: Why did Aiko open her mouth after watching Nour?
qa.a: Seeing Nour enjoy the ice made it seem safe, so Aiko felt curious enough to try.

qa.q: What could Aiko's father try with the next new food?
qa.a: Let her watch another child, or himself, enjoy it first, then offer a small taste.

qa.q: What might Nour's mother notice?
qa.a: She may notice Aiko watching and feel amused that Nour's giggles helped another child try it.

grounding: Shows a toddler at a summer festival tasting a new food only after watching another child eat it happily.

passage:
Monday, a cold December morning at the crèche. Alka pushed away the bowl of mashed sweet potato. 'No!'

Wednesday. Lavanya sat beside her, scooping orange mash into her mouth and humming, smearing it on her cheeks. Alka watched the spoon go up and down. She touched the mash with one finger.

Friday. Lavanya said, 'Yum!' and opened her mouth wide. Alka picked up her own spoon, took a tiny bite, then another, and banged the bowl for more.

qa.q: What food did Alka push away on Monday?
qa.a: The bowl of mashed sweet potato.

qa.q: What does Alka touching the mash with one finger on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was curious but still cautious, starting to trust the food after watching Lavanya enjoy it.

qa.q: How could the crèche staff help a child try a new food?
qa.a: They could seat the child beside a friend who enjoys the food and let the child watch, without forcing a bite.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had made a face at the sweet potato?
qa.a: Alka would probably have stayed wary and kept pushing the bowl away, since Lavanya's enjoyment was what signalled it was safe.

grounding: A toddler tries a new food only after watching another child eat it happily over several days.

passage: In the Ludhiana flat, Mehak sat in her high chair, lips shut tight against the spoon of dal-khichdi. Mummy sighed. Then cousin Himani, four, climbed onto the chair opposite with her own bowl. 'Mmm! Khichdi!' She ate a big spoonful, swinging her legs. Mehak stared. Himani ate another. Mehak opened her mouth, and Mummy slipped the spoon in. Mehak chewed, then pointed at both bowls, grinning. Himani clapped. 'She likes it like me!'

qa.q: What was on the spoon Mehak refused?
qa.a: Dal-khichdi.

qa.q: Why did Mehak open her mouth after watching Himani?
qa.a: Seeing Himani eat happily made the khichdi seem safe and good, so Mehak felt trusting and curious enough to try.

qa.q: What could Mummy try at the next meal with a new food?
qa.a: She could seat Mehak near Himani or another child who enjoys the food, so Mehak can watch before tasting.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Mehak started eating?
qa.a: Himani felt proud and delighted, clapping and saying Mehak likes it just like her.

grounding: A toddler refuses a food until she sees her cousin eat it happily, then tries it herself.

passage:
'Swati, try the mango, baby.'
'No-no.' Swati turned her face away.
'She won't,' said her brother Arjun. 'She never eats new stuff.'
Next door's Shalini toddled over. 'Mango!' She grabbed a slice and sucked it noisily, juice down her chin.
Swati watched. 'Mango?'
'Yes, mango,' said Amma.
Swati took a slice, licked it, then bit. 'Mmm!'
Arjun's mouth fell open. 'Amma, I tried for a week!'
Amma laughed. 'She needed to see a friend do it.'

qa.q: Who grabbed a mango slice first?
qa.a: Next door's Shalini grabbed a slice and sucked it noisily.

qa.q: What made Swati willing to try the mango?
qa.a: Watching Shalini enjoy it made the mango seem safe, so Swati felt curious and brave enough to lick and bite a slice.

qa.q: What could Amma do next time Swati refuses a new food?
qa.a: Amma could invite Shalini or another child to eat it nearby, letting Swati watch first.

qa.q: How does Arjun feel when Swati finally eats the mango?
qa.a: Arjun is surprised and a little frustrated, since his week of trying failed where one friend's example worked.

grounding: A toddler tries mango only after watching another child eat it happily, while her brother reacts in surprise.
